siftei_kohen.en:
Reuven, etc. This ruling requires study. In any event, it appears to me to be an unresolved question of law, and if the creditor seized property it is not removed from him, as I shall explain. Baal HaTerumot derives this ruling from the discussion at the end of the chapter Yesh Nochalin concerning a woman who borrowed and consumed the money and then married, where the Gemara asks whether the husband is treated as a purchaser or as an heir, and concludes that he is a purchaser. This accords with the ruling of the Rif. Rashbam, however, rules in the name of Rabbenu Chananel, and agrees with him, that in such a case the husband is treated as an heir because otherwise the creditor suffers a loss. The Tur cites both views in Even HaEzer, siman 91, while the Mechaber rules without qualification like the Rif and the Rosh. In my view this requires study. If the creditor seized property he may say, "I rely upon Rabbenu Chananel and Rashbam." A careful study of the sugya indicates that their view is primary. The Mordechai, Hagahot Ashri in the name of Rabbenu Baruch, Rabbi Eliezer bar Natan, Tosafot in Nedarim, and Hagahot Ashri in the name of Raavyah all support this ruling. Piskei Rekanti likewise records the dispute and concludes in the name of Maharam that, since the authorities disagree, property already seized is not removed on account of doubt. Thus the very case of a woman who borrowed and consumed the money is an unresolved question of law. The Beit Yosef in Even HaEzer cites only Rashbam in the name of Rabbenu Chananel and does not mention these other authorities. Had he seen them, he might not have ruled as he did. Moreover, even the Rif and Rosh did not declare it certain that the husband is a purchaser. The Gemara left the question unresolved. They ruled that the creditor may not collect from the husband because the husband is in possession, and because the creditor who lent orally to a woman who was likely to marry brought the loss upon himself. Their language, "the question was not resolved; therefore an oral creditor does not collect from the husband," shows that the ruling rests upon doubt and possession. Accordingly, if the creditor seized property, it is not removed from him. Baal HaTerumot also rules in the present case, where the document lacked an after-acquired-property clause, only because the husband is in possession, not because the husband's status as purchaser is certain. The Rambam, Tur, and Mechaber likewise often state the practical ruling without qualification where the underlying Gemara remains unresolved, because the possessor prevails. The Maggid Mishneh expressly distinguishes the clear case of a written loan from the unresolved case of an oral loan. I later found that Maharam Alshich, responsum 17, states explicitly that even according to the Rif and Rosh, if the creditor seized property in the case of a woman who borrowed and consumed the money, it is not removed from him. In the present case, however, the loan to Reuven was documented, but the document omitted an after-acquired-property clause. Here there is even greater reason to permit the creditor to retain property. The rationale of the Rif, as explained by the responsa of Rashba and Ramban, is that an oral lender to a woman likely to marry should have anticipated that the husband could claim that she had repaid. That rationale does not apply to a properly documented loan to Reuven. Even according to the Mordechai's broader formulation, the oral lender should have anticipated her marriage, since she was always capable of marrying. A lender to Reuven himself cannot reasonably be said to have forfeited his money merely because he failed to include an after-acquired-property clause. Baal HaTerumot, the Tur, and the Mechaber apparently maintain that he nevertheless brought the loss upon himself by omitting that clause, but this is not the primary reasoning, particularly if the husband is treated as an heir. Still, I am not worthy to reject their ruling and that of the later authorities. For practical law, however, it appears clear that where the document simply omitted an after-acquired-property clause, the matter is at least doubtful and property seized by the creditor is not removed from him, for some authorities hold that responsibility for after-acquired property is included through a scribal presumption even when not written. Indeed, even if the document expressly stated that future acquisitions would not be encumbered, if the creditor seized property now held by the husband, it is not removed from him for the reasons stated above. It also follows that Baal HaTerumot, the Tur, and the Mechaber discuss nichsei melog, contrary to the Sema, who understands the passage as referring to nichsei tzon barzel. The ruling is derived from the question whether a husband is a purchaser, a question relevant to nichsei melog. With nichsei tzon barzel, where the husband accepts responsibility, everyone agrees that he is treated as a purchaser. The language "property she brought into the marriage" is equally appropriate to nichsei melog when the husband did not accept responsibility. The Sema's objection from siman 103 has already been answered there. See the responsum of Mahari ibn Lev, book 1, principle 12, responsum 74, at length.
And she then married, etc. The wording is not intended to limit the ruling to a woman who borrowed before marriage and only afterward married. Baal HaTerumot uses this formulation because he derived the law from the case of a woman who borrowed, consumed the money, and then married. The same ruling applies where she was already married and Reuven then died. According to this view, the creditor may not collect from the husband because the husband is treated as a purchaser. This is evident from the end of the chapter Mi SheHayah Nasui and from the Tur, Even HaEzer, siman 91. See the responsa of Maharit, simanim 9, 33, and 34, and Maharshadam, siman 189.
He is his wife's property. A.C. C.C. and M.S

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: ועמדה ונשאת וכו' הרב הש"ך טען על זה שני טענות אחד דעתו דלכך מלוה ע"פ אינו גובה מבעל דהוי כלוקח אף דאמרינן במקום פסידא שווינהו רבנן כיורש משום דטענין לבעל אולי נפרע ונסתייע לזה מתשובת רמב"ן סי' נ"ו וא"כ כאן דיש שטר רק דליכא דאקני א"כ הא א"י לטעון פרעתי והרי הבעל כיורש ועוד טען שם במלוה ע"פ אמרינן איהו אפסיד אנפשיה דלא ה"ל למזיף בלי שטר אבל כאן שלקח שטר וכי בשביל שלא כתבו דאקני יהיה נקרא אפסיד אנפשיה. והנה בטענה ראשונה נראה ברור דכל פלפול בגמרא בלותה ואכלה אי בעל כלוקח או כיורש לא איירי במלוה שמצי לטעון פרעתי דאל"כ לו יהיה דבעל יורש נטען פרעתי ואי דהאשה מודה לאו כל כמיניה לחוב לבעל בהודאתה וזהו פשוט ואפילו ר"ח וסייעתו דס"ל שוינהו אף למלוה ע"פ כיורש מודים דאין האשה נאמנת לחוב בהודאתו לבעל וגם מה פשיט הגמ' מהך דאלמנתו נזונית מנכסיו שם ליכא חשש פרעון משא"כ מלוה ע"פ אלא ברור דגמרא איירי בהך גוונא דליכא חשש פרעון ומ"מ אסיק הרי"ף וסייעתו דגבי מלוה ע"פ כלוקח שוינהו רבנן ולכן ברור דבתשובת הרמב"ן הנ"ל השיב לרווחא דמילתא כי לא הכריע אי הלכה כרי"ף או כר"ח וסייעתו דאף למלוה ע"פ שוינהו כיורש ולכך כתב בנדון המושאל דאיכא חשש פרעון לכ"ע לא גבי' וזה מורה לשונו שם אפילו נימא כיורש שוינהו רבנן ע"ש. ודע כי תשובה ההוא לא מבטן רשב"א יצא כי בתשובה ההוא היה המדפיס מאסף מגאונים רבי' והדפיסן כנראה בהקדמה שם. דרשב"א ס"ל במקום דכתבינן מטלטלין וקרקע אפילו בלי אגב גובין מיתומים מדינא כמש"ל סי' ק"ז ובתשובה ההוא נאמר בפי' דכל זמן דלא נכתב בשטר אגב אין גובה מבעל ומשמע שם להדיא אפילו הוי יורש כמבואר בלשונו וגם הא לא שייך לשיטתו דפרע דהא יש לו שטר וא"כ כיורש שוינהו וש"מ דס"ל כשיטת התום' הנ"ל דאפילו בזה לא גבי מיורש וגם כתב להדיא דמטלטלין לא גבי מבעל אפילו הוי יורש ואי' איפא תקנת גאונים וע"כ דס"ל כר"ת לעיל סי' ק"ז דלאו בכל גווני תקנו הגאונים א"כ אין לסמוך על תשובה זו. ולעומת זה הביא רבינו ב"י בא"ע סי' תשובת רשב"א דמבואר בתוכו כמ"ש בעה"ת דאפילו בשטר דכל דלית דאקני בעל לוקח הוי ולא גבה כלל הב"ח ממנו ע"ש אבל טענה שני' של הש"ך יש בו מהטענה דמה שייך בזה אפסיד אנפשיה וכן הרב ב"ש בא"ע סי' ל"א ס"ק יוד תפס סברא זו לעיקר ובאמת מרשב"א וטור ליכא ראיה דאיהו ס"ל אף דאקני ט"ס וצ"ל דפרט להדיא שלא יגבה מדאקני א"כ פשיטא דה"ל אפסיד בידים דכתב להדיא ומחל שעבודו מה דיש בו ט"ס דלא שדי אינש זוזי בכדי אבל לדעת בעה"ת ומחבר דלא ט"ס הוא וצ"ל דאין דרך לכתוב כך ולא שייך ביה דלא שדי אינש זוזי בכדי ע"כ יפה י"ל דלא שייך ביה אפסיד אנפשיה ונראה לומר דהם מפרשים איהו דאפסיד אנפשיה אין הפי' שגרם בידים היזק לעצמו רק אנן אמרינן איהו לא חס והלוה ע"פ והא הלוה היה יכול למכור נכסיו בכל עת ויצא בפחי נפש וש"מ דלא חש על זה ואיך אנן נחוש להפסידו ולבטל תקנת חכמים דעשהו כלוקח מה שהוא בעצמו לא חש לפסידו וה"ל כמו אבידה מדעת דהא כל שעה יכול למכרו וא"כ אף כאן בדלית ליה דאקני הא הוא לא חש והיה ביד הלוה כל שעה למוכרן ולא יגבה דל"ל דאקני וא"כ איך אנן נחוש לבטל משום הפסדו תקנת חכמים דלוקח שויה וא"ש ודוק כי ברור הוא ולק"מ. והנה הש"ך כתב דאם תפס הב"ח יכול לטעון קים ליה כר"ח וסייעתו דאף במלוה ע"פ הוי כיורש ויפה כתב אלא בקרקע לא שייך תפיסה ובמטלטלין אי לית ליה מטלטלין וקרקעות דגביה מדינא מיורשים לא שייך דשוינהו כיורש דעל תקנת הגאונים לא נימא דעקרהו רבנן לתקנתם ותקנתא לתקנתא לא עבדינן ואפילו בשומא הדרא דהוא מדינא דגמרא לא עקרהו רבנן מכ"ש בתקנת גאונים:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: And she then married, etc. The Shach raises two objections. First, he understands that the reason an oral creditor cannot collect from a husband, who is treated as a purchaser, even though in a case of loss the Sages sometimes treated a husband as an heir, is that we plead for the husband that perhaps the debt was repaid. He cites Responsa Ramban no. 56 for this. If so, here there is a written document and only an after-acquired-property clause is missing. The borrower cannot plead repayment, so the husband should be treated as an heir and the creditor should collect. Second, the Shach argues that in the case of an oral loan we say the lender caused his own loss because he should not have lent without a document. But here he did take a document. Why should the mere omission of an after-acquired-property clause be called self-inflicted loss? As to the first argument, it is clear that the Gemara's entire discussion of a woman who borrowed, consumed the money, and then married, and whether the husband is treated as purchaser or heir, cannot be limited to a loan where repayment can be pleaded. If that were the only issue, then even if the husband were an heir we would still plead repayment on his behalf. If the woman admits the debt, her admission cannot prejudice her husband. This is obvious. Even Rabbenu Chananel and those who hold that the Sages treated the husband as an heir even regarding an oral loan agree that the wife's admission cannot obligate him. Further, how could the Gemara prove anything from the rule that a widow is supported from her husband's estate? There is no repayment concern there, unlike an oral loan. It is therefore clear that the Gemara discusses circumstances where repayment is not a concern, and nevertheless the Rif and those who follow him conclude that, as to an oral loan, the husband is treated as a purchaser. Accordingly, in the cited responsum Ramban merely adds the repayment argument to make the result certain, because he did not decide between the Rif and Rabbenu Chananel and those who hold that even for an oral loan the husband is treated as an heir. In the case asked of him, since repayment was also a concern, everyone agreed that the creditor could not collect. His own language indicates this when he writes, "Even if we say the Sages treated him as an heir." See there. Know also that the cited responsum did not necessarily issue from the Rashba. The printed collection assembled responsa from numerous earlier geonim, as is evident from its introduction. The Rashba himself holds that where a document expressly encumbers movables and land, even without agav, collection may be made from heirs under the law of the Gemara, as I wrote above in siman 107. Yet the cited responsum says explicitly that so long as an agav clause is absent, collection cannot be made from the husband, and its language implies this even if the husband is treated as an heir. That also cannot be explained by a repayment concern, since there is a written document. It follows that the responsum follows the view of Tosafot mentioned above, that even in this case collection is not made from heirs. It also says expressly that movables are not collected from the husband even if he is treated as an heir. Where, then, is the enactment of the Geonim that creditors collect movables from heirs? Necessarily the responsum follows Rabbenu Tam's view above in siman 107 that the Geonic enactment was not made in every circumstance. Thus one cannot rely upon this responsum as representing the Rashba's own doctrine. By contrast, the Beit Yosef in Even HaEzer cites an actual responsum of the Rashba which clearly agrees with the Baal HaTerumot: even with a written loan, if there is no after-acquired-property clause, the husband is treated as a purchaser and the creditor collects nothing from him. See there. The Shach's second argument, however, has force. Why should omission of an after-acquired-property clause be called self-inflicted loss? The Rashba and Tur themselves are not proof, because they hold that an omitted after-acquired-property clause is a scribal error. Their case must therefore be one where the document expressly excluded collection from after-acquired property. There the creditor plainly caused his own loss by expressly waiving the lien that would otherwise be supplied automatically, because a person is not presumed to throw away his money. But according to the Baal HaTerumot and Mechaber, who do not treat the omission as a scribal error, we must say that this clause is not ordinarily written, and the principle that a person does not throw away his money does not apply. Why, then, call the loss self-inflicted? It appears that they understand "he caused his own loss" differently. The phrase does not mean that he actively harmed himself. Rather, we observe that he himself did not protect against the risk. When he lent orally, the borrower could sell his assets at any moment and leave the lender with nothing. The lender accepted that risk. Why should we now protect him by canceling the Sages' enactment that treats the husband as a purchaser, when the lender himself did not care about this potential loss? It is comparable to knowingly abandoning one's property. The same logic applies where the document lacks an after-acquired-property clause. The creditor accepted that the borrower could at any moment sell later-acquired property and the creditor would be unable to collect it. Since he himself did not protect against that risk, why should we undo the rabbinic rule treating the husband as purchaser in order to save him from precisely that loss? The reasoning is clear. The Shach further writes that if the creditor seized property he can plead kim li like Rabbenu Chananel and those who hold that even for an oral loan the husband is treated as an heir. That is correct in principle. But seizure does not apply to land. As to movables, if the document did not contain a movables-and-land clause that would permit collection from heirs under strict law, one cannot invoke the later Geonic enactment through the rule that the husband is an heir. We do not say that the Sages uprooted their own enactment in order to make room for a later enactment, for we do not create an enactment upon an enactment. Even regarding return of an appraisal, which is a law of the Gemara itself, the Sages did not uproot their purchaser classification. Certainly they did not do so merely because of the Geonic enactment.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
ולא כתב למלוה דאקנה וכו' ונכסים שהניח הוא הכל ממה שקנה וירש אחרי הלואתו:
ועמדה ונשאת ה"ה שנשאת בחיי האב דסוף כל סוף תיכף בנפלה לה נכסים בירושה תיכף יד הבעל בו והוי כלקחן ממנה דתמיד ידו כיד לוקח ש"ך:
דבעל בנכסי אשתו לוקח הוי אפילו בחיים של אשתו והקשה הסמ"ע הא לעיל ס"ס ק"ג דעת רמ"א דוקא במות אשתו ולא בחיים ולכן ביקש לומר דכאן מיירי בנכסי צ"ב ולכ"ע לוקח הוי וכבר השיגו הש"ך דמקורו בבעה"ת הוא הכל מנכסי מלוג ועיין מש"ל ס"ס ק"ג בישוב קושיא זו דשומא הדרא שאני ע"ש:
לוקח הוי ואע"ג דקי"ל במקום פסידא דאחריני שוינהו רבנן כיורש זהו דלית ליה דאקני ה"ל כמלוה ע"פ ובזו לא אמרינן שוינהו כיורש ועיין תומים מ"ש בישוב טענת הש"ך ומ"מ העלה הש"ך דאם תפס בעל חוב לא מפקינן מיניה. ועיין תומים דכתבתי נכון הוא בתפס מטלטלין ויש עכ"פ מטלטלין וקרקעות אבל זולת זה לא מהני תפיסה ע"ש:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
And he did not write an after acquired property clause to the lender, etc. The property left by the debtor consists entirely of what he acquired or inherited after the loan.
And she later married. The same applies if she married during her father's lifetime. In either case, the moment property later falls to her by inheritance, her husband acquires rights in it, and he is treated as a purchaser from her because his hand is always like that of a purchaser. See Shach.
A husband is treated as a purchaser of his wife's property. This applies even during her lifetime. Sema asks that above, at the end of siman 103, Rama appears to treat the husband as a purchaser only after her death. Sema therefore attempts to explain this case as involving tzon barzel property, where everyone would treat him as a purchaser. Shach correctly objects that the source in Baal HaTerumos speaks specifically of nichsei melog. See what I wrote at the end of siman 103. The return of an appraisal is exceptional and resolves the apparent contradiction.
He is treated as a purchaser. Although in situations involving loss to others the Sages sometimes treat a husband as an heir rather than a purchaser, here the creditor lacks an after acquired property clause and is therefore comparable to an oral creditor. In such a case we do not apply the special rule treating the husband as an heir. See Tumim for my resolution of Shach's argument. Shach nevertheless concludes that if the creditor seized the property, it is not removed from him. See Tumim. I wrote that this is correct where he seized movable property and there is at least some express lien on movable and landed property. Without that, seizure does not help. See there.
